FOUNDATION · 10 topics

Probability, and the four ways it misleads you

Before any test: what a probability is, what an average hides, and the assumption that quietly breaks in every real dataset. Almost every senior-level trap further down this page is a violation of something in this block — a dependent sample, a long tail, a base rate nobody mentioned.

Practise this whole block with a chatbot

Read it first
You are my AI/ML interview tutor. This session covers ONE block of statistics and probability: Foundation — Probability, and the four ways it misleads you

The topics in this block are:
1. Bayes is a base-rate machine — Everyone can state the rule — the follow-up finds out whether you noticed the base rate is doing all the work
2. The CLT does not rescue skewed metrics — "We have well over thirty samples, so it is normal" is the most confidently wrong sentence in a stats round
3. Independence is the assumption that silently breaks — Your sample size is not the number of rows — it is the number of independent things you randomised
4. Picking the right count distribution — Your variance is three times your mean — that one fact already rules out the model most people reach for
5. Regression to the mean is not a treatment effect — If you picked the group because it was extreme, it improves whether or not you touch it
6. Correlation, causation and the third thing — Everyone can recite the slogan. The interview asks which of three structures you are looking at, and only one of them is fixed by adding the variable to your regression
7. Expected value and the linearity trick — Linearity holds whether or not the pieces are independent — that one fact solves most of the brainteasers, and the follow-up is always "now the variance"
8. Long tails break averages and break models — The mean sits in a gap where nobody lives, the median is not the business metric, and the loss you trained on quietly picked one of them for you
9. Sampling: which bias are you buying — Every dataset was collected by a process, and the process — not the row count — decides what you are allowed to conclude
10. Simulation beats recall — "I would simulate the null and look" outranks a half-remembered formula — as long as you can say what it is you would generate

01foundation

Bayes is a base-rate machine

Everyone can state the rule — the follow-up finds out whether you noticed the base rate is doing all the work

Two numbers decide whether a positive result means anything, and only one of them is the accuracy of the test. The other is how common the thing was before you tested. A model that is right ninety-nine times in a hundred sounds decisive. Point it at something that happens once in a thousand and screen a thousand cases: one case is real and the model catches it, but it also mislabels one in every hundred of the 999 that are fine, which is ten more. Eleven alarms, one of them real. Nine per cent.

Nothing about the model is broken. It is doing exactly what the accuracy figure says it does. Rare-event arithmetic is what turns a very good detector into a queue of false alarms, and it is why you cannot judge a screening system by its accuracy alone. When someone hands you a headline accuracy without a prevalence, you have been handed half a number, and the missing half is usually the bigger one.

Like a metal detector on a beach. It beeps for almost every coin and hardly ever misses one. But there are ten thousand bottle tops for every ring, so nearly everything it beeps at is rubbish. Nobody blames the detector. The beach decides what the beeps are worth.

The version worth memorising is a multiplication. Start with the odds before you tested, one in a thousand. Multiply by how much more often the model shouts for a real case than for a clean one, which here is ninety-nine to one. That leaves you at roughly one in ten, which is the nine per cent. Every further piece of genuinely new evidence multiplies again — and evidence that merely repeats what you already counted multiplies by one, which is to say it does nothing at all.

P(H∣D)=P(D∣H)P(H)/P(D), and in every interview version of this the prior dominates the answer. At 0.1% prevalence with 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity, the positive predictive value is 0.99(0.001)/[0.99(0.001)+0.01(0.999)]≈9%. The textbook screening variant — 1% prevalence, 99% sensitivity, 95% specificity — comes out at 16.7%. Neither is anywhere near 99%, and neither number moves if you improve sensitivity, because there was only ever one true case to find.

Say it in odds form and the whole family of these questions collapses to one line: prior odds × likelihood ratio = posterior odds. Prior odds 1:999, LR+=sens/(1−spec)=99, posterior odds 99:999, the same 9%. The odds form is also what makes the next question tractable: a second, conditionally independent test multiplies by 99 again, taking you to about 9.8:1, or 91%. Conditional independence is the load-bearing phrase, and it is exactly what is false when the second test is the same model re-run on the same features.

The same arithmetic runs on your experiment pipeline. At α=0.05 and 80% power, the probability that a significant result reflects a real effect is 0.8π/[0.8π+0.05(1−π)]. At a one-in-three hit rate for your ideas that is 89%; at Bing’s breakthrough rate of one in five hundred it collapses to 3.1%. The prior is not a refinement you add at the end. It is most of the answer.

You reach for it when

  • A model is reported at 99% accuracy and nobody has said how rare the event is
  • The ops team says the review queue is mostly noise and the model owner says the offline metrics are fine
  • Someone quotes a test result as if it were the probability the thing is true
  • You are asked what a second, independent check would actually buy you

The trap

Saying the model is ninety-nine per cent accurate and stopping there. Or flipping the question round: because the test is right ninety-nine times in a hundred, there is a ninety-nine per cent chance this flagged account is fraud. That sentence swaps the two directions of the question and never mentions how rare fraud was to begin with.

"The model is 99% accurate, so a flagged account is 99% likely to be fraud." That is the prosecutor’s fallacy with a dashboard attached — it swaps P(flag∣fraud) for P(fraud∣flag). The quieter half of the trap is quoting precision measured on a rebalanced test set: a 90% precision figure from a set that is half fraud tells you nothing at all about a stream that is 0.05% fraud.

The math a prior you have to defend out loud

prior odds 1:999P(¬H)P(H)​​​×LR+=99P(D∣¬H)P(D∣H)​​​=≈1:10P(¬H∣D)P(H∣D)​​​Two independent pieces of evidence multiply their likelihood ratios. Two correlated ones do not, and the second is worth far less than 99 — often worth exactly 1.

Where the thousand accounts go, and what a second pass buys no dependencies

prev, sens, spec = 0.001, 0.99, 0.99

tp = prev * sens              # 0.00099 -- the one real case, caught
fp = (1 - prev) * (1 - spec)  # 0.00999 -- ten clean accounts, flagged
print(tp / (tp + fp))       # 0.090. nine per cent of the queue is real

# the same thing in odds, which is the form that scales
prior = prev / (1 - prev)   # 1 : 999
lr    = sens / (1 - spec)   # 99
print(prior * lr)           # 0.099, so 9 per cent
print(prior * lr * lr)      # 9.81, so 91 per cent -- but ONLY if the two
                              # tests are conditionally independent. Re-running
                              # the same model on the same features is not.

Where this bites in production

R v Sally Clark (UK, 1999). Roy Meadow testified that the chance of two cot deaths in one family was "1 in 73 million", multiplying two probabilities that were not independent and never once comparing the figure against the prior odds of a mother murdering two of her children. Clark served three years; the conviction was quashed in 2003 and the Royal Statistical Society issued a formal protest in 2001. Both failures on this card — a missing base rate and an assumed independence — inside a single sentence spoken in court.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Your screening model is 99% accurate on a one-in-a-thousand event, so only 9% of its alerts are real. The team proposes running it twice. What does the second pass buy you?
Nothing, unless the second check looks at something new. The first pass moves the odds from one in a thousand to about one in ten. A genuinely separate check with the same hit rate would multiply again and take you to roughly nine in ten. But running the same model over the same data twice just repeats itself, so it multiplies by one and you have gained nothing. What earns the improvement is a different kind of evidence — the device, the payment network, a human reviewer — not a second look at the same thing.
Nothing as described — and a great deal if the second test is genuinely independent. In odds form the first pass takes 1:999 to about 1:10 by multiplying in a likelihood ratio of 99. A second pass multiplies by 99 again, giving roughly 9.8:1, about 91%. That factor exists only under conditional independence given the true label. Re-running the same model on the same features has LR≈1: it repeats evidence you already counted. What earns the second 99 is a different signal source — device history, a payment-network check, a human reviewer. Multiplying dependent evidence is precisely the Sally Clark error.
Your fraud model shows 90% precision on the test set. Fraud is 0.05% of live traffic. What will the ops team actually see, and what do you change?
A review queue that is almost all false alarms. The ninety per cent figure came from a test set where fraud had been made artificially common, and it does not survive contact with traffic where fraud is one case in two thousand. Recompute the hit rate at the real rate first. Then either raise the bar so the model only shouts about the cases it is most sure of, sized to what the team can actually review, or add a second check that looks at different evidence entirely.
A queue that is almost entirely false positives, and the test set is why you did not see it coming. A 90% precision figure measured on a balanced or negatively-downsampled set does not transfer; recompute the positive predictive value at the true 0.05% prevalence and it collapses by orders of magnitude. Three moves, in order: raise the threshold and report precision@k at the volume ops can genuinely review; add a cheap second stage built on independent features; and change the reported metric from precision on a curated set to precision at the operating point on live traffic.
An A/B result comes back significant at the 5% level with 80% power. How likely is the effect real?
You cannot say without knowing how often your ideas work at all. If about a third of what your team tries is genuinely good, then close to nine in ten significant results are real. If only one idea in five hundred is a breakthrough, as at Bing, then only about three in a hundred significant results are real and the rest are noise that cleared the bar. The rate at which your team has good ideas is the missing input, and it matters more than the test does.
Unanswerable without the base rate, which is the whole point of the question. The positive predictive value is 0.8π/[0.8π+0.05(1−π)], where π is the share of your ideas that are genuinely good. At π=1/3 that is 89%; at Bing’s breakthrough rate of π=1/500 it is 3.1%. So the honest answer names π for your own team: if nine in ten of your experiments come back flat, most of your significant results are noise, and the moves that help are better hypotheses, more power, and replicating anything surprising.

Say this back tomorrow

Start with how common the thing is, then multiply by how much louder the model shouts for a real case than a clean one. That product, not the accuracy, is your answer.
prior odds×LR+=posterior odds  ·  1:999×99≈1:10
  • Accuracy without prevalence is half a number — ask for the base rate first
  • Odds form makes it one multiplication, and makes the independence assumption visible
  • A second check only multiplies again if it looks at genuinely new evidence

02foundation

The CLT does not rescue skewed metrics

"We have well over thirty samples, so it is normal" is the most confidently wrong sentence in a stats round

The rule everyone half-remembers says averages settle into a neat bell shape once the sample is big enough. That is true, with a catch nobody quotes: how big is big enough depends entirely on how lopsided your data are. Money metrics are the most lopsided things you own. Revenue per user is mostly zeros with a handful of people spending thousands, and the average of a hundred such users is still visibly lopsided, nothing like a bell.

The consequence is practical rather than theoretical. Every interval and every test you run on that average quietly assumes the bell shape has already arrived. When it has not, the error rates your software prints are not the ones you are getting, and an experiment that looks flat may simply be far too small to see anything. Microsoft’s experimenters put a number on it: for their revenue-per-user metric you need over a hundred thousand people in each arm before the maths behaves, and most teams budget a small fraction of that.

Like waiting for a queue to average out. Most people at the counter take a minute. Once an hour, someone takes forty. Average ten customers and that one visit swamps everything; average ten thousand and it barely registers. The service is identical either way. Only the number of people decides whether the average can be trusted.

You have two honest ways out, and both are decisions rather than tricks. Cap the metric at a level you announce before you look at the data — capping revenue per user at Bing cut its lopsidedness from eighteen to about five, which cut the users needed by roughly eleven times — or measure something bounded instead, such as whether a person bought at all rather than how much they spent. Capping trades a little bias for a lot of precision. That is a fair trade, and it stops being fair the moment you choose the cap after seeing the result.

The theorem is a statement about the sampling distribution of Xˉ, not about your data, and the rate of convergence is governed by skewness: skew(Xˉ)=s/n​. Kohavi’s Rule 7 turns that into a number you can use in a planning meeting — you need at least 355s2 users per arm before the t-test’s normal approximation is trustworthy, where s is the skewness coefficient. Bing’s Revenue/User has s=17.9, so 355×17.92≈114,000 per arm, and that only buys 4.4% sensitivity.

Nearly every metric with money or time in it is heavy-tailed: revenue per user, session length, items per order, tokens per request, LLM latency. Offer the fixes in this order. Cap or winsorise at a pre-declared percentile — capping at Bing took s from 18 to 5.3, and 355×5.32≈10,000, an elevenfold cut in the sample required. Switch to a bounded proxy such as purchaser rate. Bootstrap the interval. Or change the randomisation and analysis unit. Capping buys variance reduction with bias, which is a decision you state before launch, never after seeing the lift.

Two diagnostics that do not work. Shapiro–Wilk on the raw data answers the wrong question and, at n in the hundreds of thousands, rejects every time — you need normality of the sampling distribution, not of the data. And a histogram of the metric says nothing directly about the distribution of its mean. What does work: bootstrap the mean and look at the shape you get, and run A/A tests to check the false positive rate lands near 5%.

You reach for it when

  • The metric has money, time or tokens in it and the team wants a t-test
  • A revenue-per-user experiment came back flat after two weeks and someone calls it a null
  • Somebody justifies a test with "we have well over thirty samples"
  • You are asked how long to run a revenue experiment and the honest answer feels absurdly long

The trap

Reaching for a rank-based test because the data are not bell-shaped, then reporting the outcome as a percentage lift in revenue. Rank tests answer whether one group tends to come out ahead of the other. Revenue is a total, and a total is built out of an average. You have quietly answered a different question from the one the business asked, and the number you hand over cannot be defended.

"The data are not normal, so I will use Mann–Whitney." The U test asks whether one group stochastically dominates the other; the business asked about total revenue, which is a mean. You have changed the question without announcing it, and the percentage lift you report afterwards cannot be derived from the test you ran. The mirror-image trap is "40,000 per arm, way past 30" — the 30 rule has no skewness term in it, and at s=17.9 you are still four times short.

The math skewness measured on your own metric, before the test

skew(Xˉ)=n​s​⟹n≳355s2per armThe 355 is a rule of thumb calibrated for a t-test at 5% with the tails behaving. The s2 is not negotiable: halving the skewness quarters the sample you need.

Has the bell shape arrived on your metric yet? numpy, scipy

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# rev: one row per user, revenue over the period
s = stats.skew(rev)
print(s, 355 * s**2)   # skewness, and the users per arm it demands

# the honest check: is the SAMPLING distribution symmetric yet?
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = rng.integers(0, len(rev), size=(20000, 100))
print(stats.skew(rev[idx].mean(axis=1)))
# about s / sqrt(100). at s = 17.9 that is 1.8 -- still miles off

Where this bites in production

Microsoft’s Seven Rules of Thumb for Web-Site Experimenters (KDD 2014) exists because Bing teams repeatedly shipped and killed features on underpowered revenue metrics. Rule 7 is written as a direct correction, with a table of 355 times the squared skewness alongside per-metric sensitivities: Revenue/User at a skewness of 17.9 needs about 114,000 users per arm just to reach 4.4% sensitivity, and capping the metric cut skewness from 18 to 5.3, an elevenfold cut in the users required. Those figures came off their own platform, not out of a textbook.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Bookings per user is heavily right-skewed with a big spike at zero, and the team wants a t-test. What do you do?
Work out how many users the lopsidedness demands before you argue about the test. The spike at zero is not the problem; the long tail is. Multiply the squared lopsidedness of the metric by 355 and compare that with the users you have in each arm. Clear it and the ordinary test is fine. Miss it and you cap the metric at a level you announce now, or you split the question in two: what share of people booked at all, and how much the bookers spent. What you must not do is switch to a rank-based test and then report a percentage lift.
Work out 355s2 before arguing about the test. The spike at zero is not the problem; the tail is. If you have far more than 355s2 users per arm, the t-test is fine and the zeros are irrelevant. If you do not, offer three things in order: cap at a percentile you declare now, which is what Bing did to take s from 18 to 5.3 and the requirement from about 115,000 to about 10,000 per arm; split the metric into a bounded conversion rate and a conditional amount, which is often the decomposition the business wanted anyway; or bootstrap the interval. Do not switch to Mann–Whitney and then quote a mean lift.
Someone says we have 40,000 users per arm, which is well past 30, so the central limit theorem applies. What is wrong?
The thirty rule says nothing about lopsidedness, and lopsidedness is the entire problem. The number of users you need grows with the square of how lopsided the metric is. For a metric as skewed as revenue per user at Bing the bar is about 114,000 people per arm, so 40,000 is roughly a third of what is needed and every interval you print is narrower than the truth. Measure the lopsidedness of your own metric, then split the control group at random and check that a test on the two halves comes back exciting about one time in twenty.
The 30 rule contains no skewness term, and skewness is the entire problem. The mean’s skewness is s/n​, so the sample you need scales with s2. At s=17.9 the bar is 355×17.92≈114,000 per arm, so 40,000 is roughly a third of what is needed and your interval’s coverage is not 95%. Two moves that follow: measure s on the metric instead of assuming it, and run an A/A test — if the false positive rate comes back well above 5%, the approximation has demonstrably not arrived.
Revenue per user has a skewness of 18 and you have 30,000 users per arm. Name your options and pick one.
You are four times short, so cap the metric and announce the rule before you look. The lopsidedness you have demands roughly 115,000 users in each arm and you have 30,000. Running four times longer is the honest alternative and usually is not available. Capping the metric at a high level brings the requirement down to around 10,000, which you comfortably clear. The price is that you are no longer measuring the true average, so fix the cap before the test starts and show both the capped and the uncapped result.
You are four times short, so cap, and say the rule out loud now. 355×182≈115,000 per arm against the 30,000 you have. Option one is to run roughly four times longer, which is rarely on offer. Option two is capping: Bing’s cap took skewness to 5.3, and 355×5.32≈10,000, which you clear three times over. The cost is bias — you are no longer estimating the true mean — so fix the percentile before launch and report capped and uncapped lifts side by side. Choosing the cap afterwards is a researcher degree of freedom and it will be found.

Say this back tomorrow

Multiply the squared lopsidedness of your metric by 355. That is how many users you need in each arm before the ordinary test is safe.
n≳355s2  ·  s=17.9⇒n≈114,000  ·  s=5.3⇒n≈10,000
  • The theorem is about the average, not the data, and its speed is set by skewness
  • Capping buys precision with bias — declare the rule before launch, never after
  • A rank test answers a different question from the one revenue is asking

03foundation

Independence is the assumption that silently breaks

Your sample size is not the number of rows — it is the number of independent things you randomised

Every interval and every test you run rests on one quiet assumption: that each row you counted is a fresh, unrelated piece of information. Real data almost never is. One user generates forty sessions. Two hundred evaluation questions come from twenty source documents. Comments sit inside threads and requests sit inside customer accounts. Rows from the same group resemble each other, so the second row from a user tells you much less than the first did.

When that happens your uncertainty comes out too small, which makes your result look too impressive, which means you ship noise. The nasty part is that nothing looks wrong. There is no error, no warning, just a confident number arriving on time. The habit that saves you is to ask out loud what actually got randomised. If you randomised users, your sample size is users, no matter how many rows the query returned.

Like asking households what they had for dinner. Interview four households and you have four dinners. Interview one household of four and you have one dinner described four times. The transcript is the same length either way, and only one of them is worth four.

You can put a price on it. If each user hands you fifty events and events within a user resemble each other even mildly — a correlation of about a fifth — then two million rows carry roughly as much information as two hundred thousand independent ones, and the uncertainty you should be quoting is about three times what the naive calculation prints. Every fix says the same thing in a different dialect: work at the level you randomised. Roll the data up to one number per user, or use a method that knows which rows belong together when it draws the error bars.

Every t-test, interval and p-value assumes Var(∑Xi​)=∑Var(Xi​), which holds only under independence. When observations cluster the covariance terms are positive and your variance estimate is missing them, so the standard errors come out too small — in production analytics typically by a factor of 2 to 5. The scale factor is the design effect 1+(m−1)ρ, with m the cluster size and ρ the intraclass correlation. At m=50 events per user and ρ=0.2 the design effect is 10.8, so two million rows behave like about 185,000 and every SE is 10.8​=3.3 times what you printed.

Four fixes, all the same idea in different clothes. Cluster-robust standard errors. The delta method for ratio metrics such as clicks per impression, with all moments computed at the user level — provably equivalent to the cluster-robust estimator for clustered randomised experiments. Bootstrap at the cluster level rather than the row level. Or aggregate to the randomisation unit first and test the per-unit values, which changes the estimand from a ratio of averages to an average of ratios, so say which one the business is asking for before you pick it.

The same failure has a different name on every team. Session metrics under user randomisation. Per-query metrics under per-user assignment. Tenant randomisation in B2B, where you have hundreds of clusters instead of millions of users. Eval questions drawn from shared source passages. The diagnostic is identical in all four: count the clusters rather than the rows, and treat an A/A test that fires far more than 5% of the time as evidence you have found one.

You reach for it when

  • You randomised users and the analysis is per event, per session or per impression
  • An eval set draws several questions from each source document
  • Your A/A test comes back significant far more often than one time in twenty
  • A B2B experiment randomises accounts and then reports per-seat numbers

The trap

"We have two million rows, so we have plenty of power." You have forty thousand users. The subtler version of the same mistake is resampling rows when you bootstrap: shuffling individual rows quietly re-imposes independence at the exact step where you were trying to measure the dependence, so the interval comes out just as narrow and just as wrong. Resample whole users.

"I have 2 million rows, so I have tons of power." You have 40,000 users. The subtler version, which gets past more interviewers: bootstrapping rows in clustered data. Resampling individual rows re-imposes independence at exactly the step where you were trying to measure the dependence, so the bootstrap interval comes out just as narrow as the wrong analytic one and looks like it was earned. Resample clusters.

The math needs a cluster id on every row

DEFF=1+(m−1)ρneff​=DEFFn​SEtrue​=DEFF​SEnaive​ρ is the correlation between two rows from the same cluster, and it only has to be small. At 50 rows per user, ρ=0.2 already costs you a factor of eleven in effective sample size.

The same data, two standard errors statsmodels

import statsmodels.api as sm

# 40,000 users x 50 impressions = 2,000,000 rows, one binary click
X = sm.add_constant(df["treated"])

naive = sm.OLS(df["click"], X).fit()
clust = sm.OLS(df["click"], X).fit(
    cov_type="cluster",
    cov_kwds={"groups": df["user_id"]})

print(naive.bse[1], clust.bse[1])  # the second is 2-5x the first
print(df["user_id"].nunique())      # this, not len(df), is your n

Where this bites in production

Anthropic’s Adding Error Bars to Evals (arXiv:2411.00640, November 2024) makes clustered standard errors recommendation number two of five, and prints the explicit formula, because eval suites draw several questions from the same source passage and naive standard errors understate the uncertainty on published model comparisons. The production version is the same arithmetic: naive standard errors run 2 to 5 times too small whenever the randomisation unit and the analysis unit differ, the case Microsoft’s experimentation group published on for tenant-randomised B2B tests.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

You randomised by user but you are analysing click-through rate per impression. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
You counted impressions but you randomised people, so the error bars are fiction. Every impression from one person moves with the others, so treating each as fresh evidence makes the result look two to five times more certain than it is, and your sanity checks will fire constantly. Fix it by computing at the person level: either use a method that knows which rows share a person, or work out each person’s own rate first and compare those. The second choice quietly changes what you are measuring — the average person’s rate rather than the overall rate — so decide which the business is asking about.
Your denominator is impressions and your unit of randomisation is users, so the standard error is fiction. Impressions within a user are correlated, so a two-proportion z-test with n set to impressions understates the SE, typically by 2 to 5 times, and your A/A tests will fire constantly. Two correct fixes: the delta method for the ratio Xˉ/Yˉ with every moment computed at the user level, or cluster-robust standard errors, which are provably equivalent here. Averaging each user’s own ratio and t-testing those is also valid but estimates the average of ratios, not the ratio of averages. Say which one the OEC is.
Two million rows, forty thousand users, fifty events each. How much power do you actually have?
Nothing like two million observations’ worth. With fifty events per person, rows inside a person repeat each other. Even a mild resemblance between them — a correlation of about a fifth — shrinks two million rows to the equivalent of roughly two hundred thousand and triples every error bar, so the smallest effect you can detect is three times bigger than you planned for. Report how many people, not just how many rows, and measure the resemblance from your own data rather than assuming it away.
Far less than the row count suggests — compute the design effect before you answer. 1+(m−1)ρ with m=50; even a mild ρ=0.2 gives 10.8. Effective sample size is 2,000,000/10.8≈185,000, and every SE is 10.8​=3.3 times the naive one, so an MDE computed off the row count is wrong by the same factor. Report the number of clusters alongside the number of rows, and estimate ρ from your own data rather than guessing it — it falls out of a one-line variance-components fit.
Your eval suite is 200 questions drawn from 20 source passages, and model A beats model B by 3 points. What do you check first?
That your real sample is twenty passages, not two hundred questions. Questions drawn from one passage share its topic, its difficulty and any mistakes buried in it, so they are not twenty times more informative than the passage itself. Redraw the error bars grouping by passage, or resample whole passages rather than single questions. Then win the power back the cheap way: score both models on exactly the same items and compare them question by question, which cancels out how hard each question was.
That your n is 20, not 200. Questions from one passage share its topic, its difficulty and any label noise in it, so the effective sample size sits near the number of passages rather than the number of questions. Compute clustered standard errors with the passage as the cluster, which is Anthropic’s recommendation number two, or bootstrap passages rather than questions. Then buy the power back: run both models on identical items and test the paired per-question difference, which removes item-difficulty variance entirely and is usually worth more than any of the corrections.

Count the things you randomised, not the rows. Fifty rows per person at a mild within-person correlation costs you a factor of eleven.
DEFF=1+(m−1)ρ  ·  m=50, ρ=0.2⇒DEFF=10.8  ·  SE×3.3
  • The randomisation unit is the sample size, whatever the query returns
  • Naive standard errors run 2 to 5 times too small when rows cluster
  • Bootstrap clusters, never rows — row resampling repeats the same lie

04foundation

Picking the right count distribution

Your variance is three times your mean — that one fact already rules out the model most people reach for

Counting things looks like the simplest measurement there is, and it is where the most avoidable modelling errors live. A count comes from one of a small number of physical stories, and each story implies a different amount of natural variation. A fixed number of chances with the same chance each time gives one shape. Events arriving over a window at a steady rate gives another. Drawing a handful of items from a small pool without putting them back gives a third, because the pool changes as you draw.

The useful diagnostic takes one line of code and no theory at all. Compute the average of your counts, then compute the variance — how spread out they are. For the steady-arrivals story those two should come out roughly equal. That is a defining property of the story, not a coincidence. If the spread is three times the average, the story is wrong, and the usual reason is that you are not looking at one population: some users do the thing far more than others. Choosing on that comparison rather than on habit is the whole skill.

Like counting buses. If they turn up at random at six an hour, the number in any given hour clusters tightly around six. If half the routes are hourly and half run every ten minutes, you get quiet hours and swamped hours, and the count swings far wider than the average predicts. Same average, different spread, because there is more than one kind of route.

Four stories are worth being able to name on demand. A fixed number of tries at the same chance. Events arriving over a window at a steady rate. Drawing without replacement from a pool small enough that removing items matters. And the wider-spread version of the arrivals story, for when the rate itself differs from one person to the next. Interviewers pick the case where the obvious answer is wrong, and the two features that make it wrong are a small pool and a natural ceiling. Read the setup for those two before you name anything.

Four physical stories, four distributions. Binomial: n fixed and known, constant p, independent trials, and Var=np(1−p)<μ. Poisson: events in continuous time at rate λ, use λt for a window, and Var=μ exactly. Hypergeometric: sampling without replacement from a finite pool, so the trials are dependent by construction. Negative binomial: a Gamma-mixed Poisson, for counts with Var>μ. Binomial(200, 0.02) is well approximated by Poisson(4) — that is the rare-event limit, and it is the Netflix form of the question.

Overdispersion is the tell you are being tested on. Var/μ=3 rules out Poisson by definition, not by goodness of fit. It nearly always means unmodelled heterogeneity — users carry different underlying rates — or clustering, which is the same problem wearing the other card’s clothes. Fit a Poisson GLM anyway and the standard errors come out deflated by roughly ϕ​≈1.7, which is enough to manufacture significance across half your coefficients. Reach for negative binomial or a mixed model; if the count also has a ceiling, the bounded analogue is beta-binomial. Underdispersion, Var<μ, is the binomial signature and is worth naming when you see it.

Before you accept overdispersion as real, rule out the boring causes: a duplicated event stream, a mixture of two populations you could simply split, zero inflation from users who could never have generated the event, and time-varying exposure you have not entered as an offset. A quasi-Poisson fit is the cheap diagnostic — it estimates the dispersion parameter directly and hands you the exact factor your naive standard errors were missing.

You reach for it when

  • You are asked for the probability of at least so many events in a window
  • Your count model fits and the standard errors look implausibly tight
  • Somebody samples a handful of users from a small pool and reaches for the binomial
  • A metric is bounded by another quantity you also measure, like clicks by impressions

The trap

Two specific ones. Treating a draw from a small pool as though each pick were independent, when taking an item out changes the odds for the next pick. And using the steady-arrivals model for something with a natural ceiling — clicks cannot exceed the number of times the thing was shown, and a model with no upper limit will cheerfully put probability on counts that could never happen.

"It is counts, so Poisson." The two specific ways that fails: sampling without replacement from a small pool, where removing a unit changes the next draw — Meta’s five-from-a-hundred question exists to catch it — and any count with a natural ceiling, where Poisson puts probability on impossible values. And the one that costs the offer: seeing Var/μ=3, fitting Poisson anyway, and reporting the p-values it prints.

The math one pass over the counts

binomial Var=np(1−p)<μ​Poisson Var=μ​neg. binomial Var=μ+rμ2​>μThe variance-to-mean ratio is a model-selection statistic, not an afterthought. Compute it first and it eliminates two of the four candidates before you fit anything at all.

The variance-to-mean check, then the model statsmodels

import statsmodels.api as sm

print(counts.mean(), counts.var())
# ratio near 1 means Poisson is plausible; 3 means it is not

pois = sm.GLM(counts, X, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit()
print(pois.pearson_chi2 / pois.df_resid)
# the dispersion parameter, estimated. 1.0 is the Poisson claim

nb = sm.GLM(counts, X, family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial()).fit()
print(pois.bse[1], nb.bse[1])
# at dispersion 3 the Poisson SE is about 1.7x too small

Where these get asked, and the number that decides each one

These are documented 2026 loop questions and each turns on one number. Uber: twelve ride requests an hour, chance of at least three in ten minutes — Poisson with a rate of 2 for that window. Meta: five users drawn from a pool of 100 that is 20 treatment and 80 control, chance of exactly two treatment — hypergeometric at 20.7%, against the binomial’s 20.5%. Netflix: why 200 trials at 2% behaves like Poisson with a mean of 4. Google: why Poisson is wrong for click-through rate, since clicks are capped by impressions and vary far more across users than Poisson allows.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Your event counts have variance three times the mean. What does that tell you, and what model do you use?
It rules out the steady-arrivals model, because that model forces the spread and the average to match. Counts that vary three times as much as their average nearly always mean your users are not one population: some do the thing far more often than others. Use the version of the model that carries an extra knob for the extra spread, or model the per-user rates directly. Then name the consequence: fitting the steady-arrivals model anyway prints error bars roughly half as wide as the truth, which turns ordinary noise into findings.
It rules out Poisson outright, because Poisson forces the variance to equal the mean. Overdispersion at that scale almost always means heterogeneity: your users carry different underlying rates, so the population is a mixture rather than one process. Negative binomial is the standard answer — a Gamma-mixed Poisson with an explicit dispersion parameter — or a mixed model if you want the per-user rates themselves. Name the consequence too: a Poisson GLM fitted anyway deflates standard errors by roughly ϕ​≈1.7. And if the count has a ceiling, use beta-binomial rather than negative binomial.
Five users are drawn from a pool of 100 that is 20 treatment and 80 control. What is the probability exactly two are treatment?
Use the without-replacement model, because taking a user out changes the odds for the next pick. The answer is just under twenty-one per cent. The simpler calculation that ignores the shrinking pool gives just over twenty and a half, so the two barely differ here — which is the point of the question. The interviewer is checking whether you noticed the pool was finite, not your arithmetic. Carry away the rule: take a small slice of the pool and the two agree, take a large slice and they do not.
Hypergeometric, not binomial — the pool shrinks as you draw. (220​)(380​)/(5100​)=20.7%. The binomial answer at p=0.2 gives 20.5%, so numerically it hardly matters here, and that is exactly the trap: the interviewer is checking whether you noticed the sampling was without replacement, not whether you can carry two decimal places. Give the rule that generalises — when the sample is a small fraction of the pool the two agree, and when it is a large fraction they diverge fast, which is the finite-population correction.
Why is Poisson the wrong model for click-through rate?
Two separate reasons, and the strong answer names both. Clicks cannot exceed the number of times something was shown, so a model with no upper limit is describing a world that does not exist. And people differ in how likely they are to click, so the counts vary far more than that model allows even inside the range it can reach. The right family is the one built on a fixed number of chances, in the version that carries an extra knob for the spread between people.
Two independent reasons, and a strong answer gives both. First the support is wrong: clicks are bounded above by impressions and Poisson has no ceiling, so it assigns probability to counts that cannot occur. Second, clicks are overdispersed across users because propensity varies from person to person, so the variance is wrong well before you reach the boundary. Binomial or beta-binomial is the right family, beta-binomial being the bounded analogue of the negative binomial. It is also why ∑clicks/∑impressions cannot be z-tested with n set to impressions — that is the clustering problem again.

Say this back tomorrow

Compare the spread with the average. Below it means a fixed number of tries, level with it means steady arrivals, above it means your population is a mixture.
Var<μ binomial  ·  Var=μ Poisson  ·  Var>μ negative binomial  ·  no replacement: hypergeometric
  • Read the setup for two features: a ceiling on the count, and a pool small enough to shrink
  • Variance over mean is a model-selection statistic — compute it before you fit
  • A Poisson fit on overdispersed counts roughly halves your standard errors and manufactures significance

  • negative binomial
  • beta-binomial
  • zero inflation
  • offset term

05foundation

Regression to the mean is not a treatment effect

If you picked the group because it was extreme, it improves whether or not you touch it

Every measurement is part real and part luck. When you pick out the worst performers you pick up two kinds of people: those who are genuinely struggling, and those who happened to have a bad week. Measure them again and the bad luck does not repeat, so the group as a whole drifts back toward the middle. Nobody did anything to them. The improvement is arithmetic, and selecting on an extreme is what guarantees it.

This is why "we coached the bottom decile and they improved twelve per cent" is not evidence that coaching works. It is not evidence that it fails either, and that is the point: the number you are holding cannot tell you which. The only thing that separates a real effect from the rebound is a comparison group picked by the same rule and left alone. If you did not keep one, the honest answer is that you cannot say, and the fix is to run it again holding back a random slice of that same decile.

Like going back to a restaurant you loved. You return because that first meal was extraordinary, and this time it is merely very good. The kitchen has not slipped. The first visit caught them on a night when everything landed and the second caught an ordinary night. Choose any experience because it was extreme and the repeat will be tamer.

The same mechanism has a business name. When you ship the experiment that measured the biggest win, you have selected partly on a lucky measurement, so what you get in production is reliably smaller than what you reported. Measured across whole portfolios the shrinkage runs twenty to fifty per cent, which is why adding up the lifts of thirty shipped experiments never matches the movement in the annual metric. Same arithmetic, different costume, and it is the second half of this card that interviewers actually push on.

Write the observed score as X=τ+ε. Selecting on X being extreme selects jointly on τ and on ε, and ε does not persist, so the conditional expectation of the second measurement is pulled toward the population mean by the reliability: E[X2​∣X1​]=μ+ρ(X1​−μ) with ρ<1. The expected rebound is (1−ρ)(μ−X1​), entirely mechanical, and it is largest exactly where the selection was most extreme and the metric noisiest — which is to say, exactly where the intervention was most likely to be aimed.

The clean diagnostic is a control group selected by the same rule and left alone. Without one, a pre-post comparison on a selected group is uninterpretable, and no covariate adjustment rescues it: conditioning on the baseline is the selection, not a correction for it. The same structure produces the winner’s curse in experimentation — Gelman and Carlin’s Type M error is the exaggeration ratio of an estimate conditional on significance, worst when the study was underpowered — and the decline effect in science. The fixes on the experimentation side are empirical-Bayes shrinkage of the reported lift, a post-launch holdback, or discounting the roadmap forecast by a measured shrinkage factor.

How to separate this from a genuine novelty effect, because interviewers push on exactly that seam: novelty shows a time trend inside the experiment window as users habituate, whereas regression to the mean does not — it is a one-off gap between the selected estimate and the truth, visible only on re-measurement. Both can be present at once, and naming only one of them is the answer that loses the point.

You reach for it when

  • An intervention was aimed at the worst-performing users, accounts or regions
  • Someone reports a before-and-after number for a group that was selected on the before
  • A shipped experiment’s lift is visibly smaller in production than it was in the test
  • The best of many candidates — a prompt, a model, a sweep — is quoted at its winning score

The trap

"We controlled for the starting point by only including users who started low." That is not a control, it is the mechanism. Filtering on a low first measurement is precisely what guarantees the second one looks better. The other version is a before-and-after chart for the selected group with no comparison group anywhere on it, and the gap labelled as the effect.

"We controlled for baseline by only including low-baseline users." That is the mechanism presented as its own remedy: conditioning on an extreme first measurement is exactly what manufactures the rebound. The second trap arrives once someone concedes the first — attributing the entire shrinkage to novelty. Novelty is a different mechanism with a different signature, and the answer that scores names both and says how to tell them apart.

The math no treatment required

E[X2​∣X1​]=μ+ρ(X1​−μ),ρ=στ2​+σε2​στ2​​<1ρ is the reliability of the measurement. The noisier the metric and the more extreme the selection, the larger the rebound — and none of it is an effect of anything.

The effect you can measure with no treatment at all numpy

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

tau = rng.normal(50, 10, 200_000)   # true ability, fixed for each user
w1  = tau + rng.normal(0, 10, 200_000)  # week 1: ability plus noise
w2  = tau + rng.normal(0, 10, 200_000)  # week 2: ability plus FRESH noise

worst = w1 < np.quantile(w1, 0.10)  # bottom decile, selected on week 1
print(w1[worst].mean(), w2[worst].mean())  # 25.2 then 37.7
print(w2[worst].mean() / w1[worst].mean() - 1)
# 0.497 -- a "+50% improvement" from an intervention that does not exist

Where this bites in production

The Open Science Collaboration’s 2015 replication project: 97% of the original studies were statistically significant, 36% of the replications were, and the average effect size roughly halved, from 0.403 to 0.197. In experimentation the same arithmetic is priced — Airbnb’s Experiment Reporting Framework documents 20 to 50% portfolio-level overstatement, and Facebook shrank estimates across 226 News Feed tests to cut mean squared error by 44%. Palmer and Pe’er (PLOS Genetics 2017) show the identical inflation in the top hits of quantitative-trait GWAS.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

We targeted the bottom decile of users with a re-engagement campaign and their engagement went up 12%. Ship it?
No — the campaign and a guaranteed rebound are tangled together in that single number. Picking the bottom tenth picks people who were genuinely disengaged and people who happened to have a quiet week, and quiet weeks do not repeat, so the group climbs on its own. Run it again holding back a random slice of that same bottom tenth and compare the two. If it has already gone out to everyone, the best you can do is check whether the next tenth up also drifted, and say plainly that this is weaker evidence.
No — you have measured a campaign and a guaranteed rebound added together, and you cannot separate them. Selecting the bottom decile selects partly on transient noise, and E[X2​∣X1​]=μ+ρ(X1​−μ) with ρ<1 means the group rises whether or not you act. The fix is one sentence: randomise a holdout inside the bottom decile and compare treated against untreated within it. If the campaign has already gone out to everyone, the salvage is to check whether the ninth decile drifted upward over the same window, and to say plainly that this is weaker than a randomised comparison.
A colleague says we controlled for baseline by restricting to low-baseline users. Is that a valid control?
No — that restriction is what creates the illusion in the first place. Choosing only people whose first score was low means choosing people who were partly unlucky, and unluckiness does not repeat. Putting the starting score into a model afterwards does not undo it, because the group was built out of that score. The move that works is to select on the starting score if you want to, and then split that selected group at random so half get the treatment and half do not.
No — that restriction is the thing that creates the artefact. Conditioning on an extreme value of a noisy first measurement is the definition of selecting on noise; it does not remove the rebound, it guarantees it. Putting the baseline into a regression has the same problem when the group itself was formed from the baseline, and there is a second failure mode lurking: adjusting for anything measured after treatment is a bad control. What works is randomisation inside the selected stratum — select on baseline if you want, then randomise within the selection.
Your test measured a 1% lift. Should you forecast 1% after launch?
No — forecast less than one per cent, and say how much less. You are shipping this test because it came out best, and coming out best means it caught a favourable run of luck as well as a real effect. Measured across whole portfolios, shipped winners deliver twenty to fifty per cent less than they measured. So discount the forecast, and keep a small randomly held-back group after launch so you can measure what you really got rather than argue about it a quarter later.
No — forecast less, and be specific about how much less. You are shipping this one because it won, which means you selected on a measurement that contains noise, so the estimate is biased upward. That is Gelman and Carlin’s Type M error, the exaggeration ratio conditional on significance, and it is worst on underpowered tests. Empirically, shipped-win effects shrink 20 to 50%, so the defensible forecast is a shrunk estimate — empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward the portfolio mean is the standard tool — plus a post-launch holdback so you measure what you actually got.

Say this back tomorrow

Extreme first, ordinary second. The further out you selected and the noisier the metric, the bigger the free improvement you are about to take credit for.
E[X2​∣X1​]=μ+ρ(X1​−μ), ρ<1  ·  rebound =(1−ρ)(μ−X1​)
  • Selecting on an extreme selects on noise, and noise does not repeat
  • A comparison group chosen by the same rule is the only clean diagnostic
  • Same mechanism as the winner’s curse: shipped lifts shrink 20 to 50%

06foundation

Correlation, causation and the third thing

Everyone can recite the slogan. The interview asks which of three structures you are looking at, and only one of them is fixed by adding the variable to your regression

Two things move together. There are only a handful of explanations, and the whole skill is telling them apart in about thirty seconds. The first caused the second. The second caused the first. Or some third thing is responsible — and that third thing comes in three quite different shapes, which is the part nobody rehearses.

A common cause sits behind both: heavy users try more features and also stick around, so the feature looks like it keeps them. A stepping stone sits on the path between them: the change works through it, so holding it fixed deletes the very effect you were measuring. A shared consequence sits downstream of both: two unrelated causes feed into it, and if you look only at the cases where it happened, you invent a link that was never there. Hold the first one fixed. Never touch the other two. The quick test is timing: did this variable already exist before you made your change, or did it appear afterwards? Before is fair game. After is a trap.

Like counting fire engines. More engines turn up, more damage — and nobody blames the engines, because the size of the fire drives both. Now survey only the buildings that burned down. Inside that group, damp weather and a slow alarm can look unrelated, or even helpful, because every building that survived has been thrown away.

Draw the arrows before you touch the data. A confounder is a common cause, X←C→Y: it opens a backdoor path and you must block it, by adjustment, stratification or randomisation. A mediator lies on the causal path, X→M→Y: conditioning on it removes exactly the effect you were trying to estimate, which is why controlling for enquiries when you measure Instant Book is Airbnb’s favourite trap. A collider is a common effect, X→K←Y: the path through it is already blocked, and conditioning on it opens it, manufacturing a correlation between two variables that were independent. That is Berkson’s paradox, and it is the one that separates candidates.

So "I controlled for it" is not an argument, it is a claim about a graph. The backdoor criterion names the minimal sufficient adjustment set; the sloppy version — put everything in and let the regression sort it out — guarantees you condition on mediators and colliders too, and can flip the sign of the estimate. The heuristic that gets you most of the way in an interview is one phrase: pre-treatment covariates only. Anything measured after the treatment is downstream of it, and downstream variables are either mediators or colliders. Neither belongs in a causal regression.

Selection into the sample is a collider you did not choose. Restricting to users who converted, sessions that completed or accounts that survived is conditioning on a common effect, and it distorts every association you then measure inside that group. The only clean fixes are randomisation or a design that makes the confounder irrelevant — instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity. A control variable is not a design.

You reach for it when

  • A dashboard says users of a feature retain far better and someone wants to build more of it
  • You are about to add a control variable "to be safe"
  • An analysis is restricted to users who converted, sessions that completed, or accounts still active
  • A promo, a notification or an email was targeted rather than randomised

The trap

Saying the slogan out loud and then, two minutes later, reading a regression coefficient as if it were an effect. The quieter version is adding more controls because more feels safer. Two of the three shapes get worse the more you control for them, and nothing in the output tells you which shape you are in.

Saying "correlation is not causation" and then, two minutes later, reading a regression coefficient as a causal effect. The sharper version is a sentence candidates volunteer unprompted: "I controlled for it, so it is causal." Ask which of the three structures the control is. If it was measured after the treatment it is a mediator or a collider, and adding it made the estimate worse, not better.

The math a graph you have to defend, not a p-value

X←C→YadjustX→M→Ydo notX→K←YneverSame three variables, three different graphs, three opposite instructions. The data cannot tell you which graph you are in. Only knowing what happened before what can.

Collider bias in six lines: nothing changes but who you look at numpy

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

skill = rng.normal(size=200_000)
luck  = rng.normal(size=200_000)  # independent by construction
print(np.corrcoef(skill, luck)[0,1])  # -0.003. nothing there

hired = skill + luck > 2.0   # a common effect of both: 7.9% get in
print(np.corrcoef(skill[hired], luck[hired])[0,1])  # -0.72 among the hired
# inside the company, talent and luck now look like substitutes.
# they are not. you conditioned on a collider.

Where this bites in production

Google Flu Trends. The model fitted 45 search terms chosen from 50 million candidates against 1,152 data points, so it learned winter rather than influenza — high-school basketball season correlates beautifully with flu season. It missed the non-seasonal 2009 H1N1 pandemic entirely, then overestimated CDC influenza-like-illness in 100 of 108 weeks from August 2011, at one point predicting more than double the true share of doctor visits. A lagged autoregression on CDC data alone beat it: mean absolute error 0.311 against 0.486. (Lazer et al., Science 343, 2014.)

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

You regress churn on promo exposure and find promos reduce churn. What is wrong?
The promos were aimed, not tossed at random, so the comparison is rigged. Whoever chose who got a promo chose using something — a predicted risk of leaving, or how engaged someone already was — and that same something drives churn on its own. You are comparing two groups that were different before the promo arrived. The fix is to hold back a slice of the targeted users at random and send them nothing.
The coefficient is a selection artefact, and you cannot sign the bias. Promos are targeted, not randomised: if the targeting model picked users predicted to churn, exposure is downstream of a churn risk score you may not even have as a column; if it picked engaged users, exposure is downstream of engagement. Either way there is an open backdoor path promo←targeting score→churn. Propose a randomised holdout inside the targeted population, or an encouragement design that randomises the nudge rather than the promo.
Estimating the effect of Instant Book on host bookings, you control for the number of enquiries. Is that OK?
No — enquiries happen because of the feature, so holding them fixed throws the answer away. Part of how Instant Book creates bookings is by changing how many enquiries come in. Freeze that and you have measured the feature with its main route to the outcome switched off. Control only for things that were already true before the feature was switched on: how old the listing is, which city, what price band.
No — enquiries are downstream of Instant Book. They are a mediator: part of how the feature produces bookings is by changing the enquiry flow, so conditioning on them strips out the effect you were hired to measure and leaves a direct effect nobody asked for. Worse, enquiries are also caused by unobserved host quality, so conditioning on them opens a collider path and biases what is left. Pre-treatment covariates only: listing age, market, price band.
Among users who converted, ad relevance and discount size are negatively correlated. Is a good ad a substitute for a discount?
No — the pattern is made by looking only at the winners. To end up in the converted group you needed either a good ad or a big discount, so within that group the people with weak ads are exactly the ones who got large discounts. The trade-off is an artefact of who you kept. Look at everyone who saw an ad and it disappears.
No — you conditioned on a collider and manufactured that correlation. Conversion is a common effect of both, relevance→convert←discount. Inside the converted group, a weak ad has to be paired with a big discount to have got there at all, so the two look like substitutes even if they were independent in the population. Recompute on everyone who saw an ad. If you want the substitution question answered, you need a design that varies one while holding the other.

Say this back tomorrow

Both arrows point out of it: hold it fixed. The arrows run through it: leave it alone. Both arrows point into it: touching it invents the link.
X←C→Y  ·  X→M→Y  ·  X→K←Y
  • A pre-treatment common cause is the only one of the three you fix by adding it to the regression
  • Anything measured after the treatment is a mediator or a collider, and both make the estimate worse
  • Conditioning on a shared consequence creates correlation between things that were independent

  • confounding
  • backdoor criterion
  • bad controls
  • Berkson’s paradox
  • difference-in-differences

07foundation

Expected value and the linearity trick

Linearity holds whether or not the pieces are independent — that one fact solves most of the brainteasers, and the follow-up is always "now the variance"

The average of a total is the total of the averages. Always. It does not matter whether the pieces are related, whether they nudge each other, whether one makes the next more likely. Work out the average of each piece and add them up. That single fact answers most of the puzzles interviewers use to find out whether you can think in probability rather than recite it.

The standard move is to chop the thing you were asked about into a pile of tiny yes-or-no events, find the chance of each, and add those chances. Ten letters shuffled into ten addressed envelopes: how many arrive correctly? Each letter has one chance in ten and there are ten letters, so on average exactly one arrives. That is true for a hundred letters and for a million. The letters are very much not independent — if nine are right the tenth must be — and it changes nothing. Where relatedness bites is the spread of outcomes, and the spread is what you get asked about next.

Like a relay team. The expected total time is the four expected leg times added together, even though the runners feed off each other and a bad handover in leg two drags leg three with it. Ask instead how unpredictable the total is, and suddenly you do have to know whether those legs move together.

Two facts, and the interview lives in the gap between them. E[∑i​Xi​]=∑i​E[Xi​] holds under any dependence at all. Var(∑i​Xi​)=∑i​Var(Xi​)+∑i=j​Cov(Xi​,Xj​) does not. So the move on nearly every brainteaser is the same: write the quantity as a sum of indicator variables, take expectations term by term, add. Dependence between the indicators is irrelevant, and you should say that out loud rather than quietly assuming it away.

The canonical setup: n letters dropped at random into n addressed envelopes, with Ii​ equal to 1 when letter i lands correctly. E[Ii​]=1/n, so the expected number of matches is n⋅1/n=1 — for every n, forever. The indicators are heavily dependent, since if n−1 match the last one must. Now the follow-up. Var(Ii​)=n1​(1−n1​) and Cov(Ii​,Ij​)=n(n−1)1​−n21​, and those covariance terms sum to exactly 1/n, so the variance is exactly 1 as well. Assume independence and you report 1−1/n: 0.9 at n=10. Close enough to pass unnoticed, wrong for a reason you should be able to name on the spot.

Two more tools finish the family. The law of total expectation, E[X]=E[E[X∣Y]], handles anything with a random stopping rule: condition on the first step and recurse. And the standard means and variances should be instant — Bernoulli p and p(1−p), Poisson λ and λ, exponential 1/λ and 1/λ2, geometric 1/p. Coupon collector falls straight out of the same decomposition: collecting all ten takes 10(1+21​+⋯+101​)≈29.3 draws, a sum of ten independent geometric waits.

You reach for it when

  • A brainteaser starts "what is the expected number of..."
  • You have produced an expectation and the interviewer says "now the variance"
  • A metric is a sum over events that are obviously not independent: sessions per user, tokens per request
  • You are about to multiply two probabilities that came from the same people

The trap

Getting the average right, then working out the spread as though the pieces were unrelated, without saying so out loud. The interviewer is not checking your arithmetic. They are listening for whether you noticed you had made an assumption.

Computing a variance as if the pieces were independent when the problem never said they were, and not flagging it. The damaging version is silent: you write down the sum of the variances and move on. In the envelope problem that hands you 0.9 instead of 1.0. On a real metric — forty sessions from the same user — it hands you a standard error that is far too small, a p-value that is far too small, and a launch decision built on noise.

The math one sum is free, the other costs you every pair

E[i∑​Xi​]=i∑​E[Xi​]Var(i∑​Xi​)=i∑​Var(Xi​)+i=j∑​Cov(Xi​,Xj​)The left equation has no assumptions attached to it. The right one has exactly one, and it is hiding in the second term: drop it and you are claiming independence you were never given.

Ten letters, ten envelopes: check the expectation and the variance numpy

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

n, trials = 10, 200_000
matches = np.array([(rng.permutation(n) == np.arange(n)).sum()
                    for _ in range(trials)])

print(matches.mean())        # 1.00 -- and it is 1.00 for every n
print(matches.var(ddof=1))  # 1.00 -- the covariance terms put the missing 1/n back
print(1 - 1/n)          # 0.90 -- what independence would have told you

Where this bites in production

Airbnb’s experimentation platform. Their own writeup opens with a price-filter test that was a significant +4% at day seven and null by the time it finished. The fix they built was a dynamic p-value threshold obtained by simulating varying real effect sizes, variances and certainty levels, rather than deriving a closed form — the honest response when the expectation you need has no clean formula behind it. (Airbnb Engineering, Experiments at Airbnb.)

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Ten letters are dropped at random into ten addressed envelopes. How many arrive correctly on average, and does your answer need them to be independent?
Exactly one, and no. Give every letter a flag that is on when it lands in the right envelope. Each flag has one chance in ten of being on, and there are ten of them, so on average one flag is on. Adding averages never requires the flags to be unrelated — and here they are wildly related, since nine correct letters force the tenth. The answer is one for a million letters too.
Exactly 1, and no. Define Ii​=1 when letter i lands correctly. Each envelope is equally likely to receive any letter, so E[Ii​]=1/10, and E[∑i​Ii​]=∑i​E[Ii​]=10⋅1/10=1 by linearity alone. The indicators are strongly dependent — nine matches force the tenth — and linearity never asked. The same argument gives 1 for any n, which is the part that surprises people.
Now compute the variance.
Also exactly one, not the nine tenths independence would give you. Add up how much each flag wobbles on its own and you get nine tenths. But the flags push each other: one letter landing right makes the others slightly more likely to land right too. Adding those interactions back contributes exactly the missing tenth. The number matters less than noticing the interactions exist.
Also exactly 1 — not the 0.9 you get by assuming independence. ∑i​Var(Ii​)=10⋅101​(1−101​)=0.9. But Cov(Ii​,Ij​)=n(n−1)1​−n21​, and there are n(n−1) such pairs, so they contribute exactly 1/n=0.1. Total: 1.0. The point is not the tenth of a unit — it is that you were asked for the assumption, and the covariance term is where it lived.
Your metric is total sessions per user over a week, and you need a standard error. Where does linearity stop helping?
At the spread, immediately. The weekly average is still just the daily averages added up, and nothing goes wrong there. The uncertainty is another matter: one heavy user contributes seven days that all look alike, so those days are not seven independent pieces of evidence. Roll the data up to one row per user before you compute uncertainty, or your error bars will be far too narrow.
At the variance, immediately. The expected weekly total is still the sum of the expected daily totals, dependence and all. The standard error is not: sessions from one user are positively correlated across days, so the covariance terms are large and positive and dropping them understates the variance badly. Aggregate to the randomisation unit first, or use cluster-robust errors, or bootstrap users rather than rows. The design effect is 1+(m−1)ρ.

Say this back tomorrow

Averages of a total always add up. Spreads only add up when the pieces do not move together.
E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]  always ·  Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y)
  • Chop the quantity into yes-or-no indicators, take each average, add — dependence never enters
  • The moment you want a variance you owe the room a covariance term or an explicit independence assumption
  • Ten letters in ten envelopes: expectation 1 for every n, and the variance is 1 too, not 0.9

  • linearity of expectation
  • indicator variables
  • law of total expectation
  • covariance
  • clustered standard errors

08foundation

Long tails break averages and break models

The mean sits in a gap where nobody lives, the median is not the business metric, and the loss you trained on quietly picked one of them for you

Some quantities are lopsided. Most requests are fast and a few are enormously slow; most customers spend a little and a few spend thousands. When a quantity looks like that, the average stops describing anybody. Half your requests can finish inside a tenth of a second while the average sits about two thirds higher, dragged up by the slow ones — and one request in a hundred takes six times the average.

Two things break as a result. First, a promise written as "the average response is under two hundred milliseconds" is comfortably true while one customer in a hundred waits nearly a second and writes in about it. What people actually feel is the slowest few percent, so that is the number that belongs in the target. Second, a model trained to minimise squared error is trying to get the average right, and in a lopsided world the average is decided by a handful of extreme rows. If the decision you care about is the typical case, or the slow tail, train something that aims at that instead.

Like the average salary in a small bar. Nine people on thirty thousand and one billionaire walk in, and the average salary in the room is now over a hundred million. Every number is correct and the average describes nobody present. Ask what the person in the middle earns, and what the top earner earns, and you have actually described the bar.

Heavy tails attack the estimate before they attack the model. The central limit theorem is about the sampling distribution of the mean, and how fast it gets there depends on skewness: Kohavi’s rule of thumb is that you need at least 355s2 users per arm, where s is the skewness coefficient. Bing’s revenue-per-user has s=17.9, which is roughly 114,000 users per arm just to reach 4.4% sensitivity. Capping the metric cut skewness from 18 to 5.3 — about an elevenfold cut in the sample size needed, bought with a bias you must declare before you look at the data, not after.

Then the two production consequences. An SLO on mean latency is satisfiable while the slowest 1% of requests are an order of magnitude worse, which is why p95 or p99 latency, never the mean, is the guardrail teams actually write down. And squared error estimates a conditional mean, so on a heavy-tailed target the loss is dominated by a handful of rows and the fit chases them: if the decision is about a typical case or a specific quantile, use absolute error or quantile (pinball) loss, or model the tail explicitly. log(1+x) is not a free lunch either — you are then estimating the mean of the logs, which exponentiates back to a geometric mean, not to revenue.

Reporting is where this costs money. You cannot exponentiate the mean of the logs and call it a revenue lift; use Duan’s smearing estimator or fit on the raw scale. And do not reach for Mann-Whitney "because the data are not normal": it tests stochastic dominance, while the business metric is a mean, so you have quietly answered a different question and nobody in the room will catch it except the interviewer.

You reach for it when

  • Someone proposes an average as a service level target
  • The metric is revenue per user, session length, items per order or tokens per request
  • A model looks excellent on validation and the money never appears
  • A team wants a t-test on bookings per user, which is zero-inflated and heavily skewed

The trap

Squashing a lopsided quantity onto a compressed scale, fitting the model there, and reporting the improvement as if it were a percentage change in money. It is not. Squashing and un-squashing does not hand back the average — it hands back a different, smaller number, and finance will notice when the revenue fails to appear.

Reporting a mean lift computed on log-transformed data as if it were a percentage lift in revenue. The sentence is usually "revenue is up 6% in the model" — it is not; the model moved the mean of the logs, which is a geometric mean and a smaller number on the raw scale. Its close cousin is "n is over thirty so the central limit theorem applies", said about a metric with a skewness of 18 and 30,000 users per arm.

The math a bias you declare in advance, in exchange for an order of magnitude

nper arm​≥355s2sBing revenue/user​=17.9⇒n≈114,000Skewness enters squared, so the metric definition is a sample-size decision. Capping took Bing from 18 to 5.3 and cut the requirement by about elevenfold without touching traffic.

The three numbers to quote instead of the mean numpy

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# latency in ms: median 95, lognormal with sigma = 1
ms = rng.lognormal(mean=np.log(95), sigma=1.0, size=2_000_000)

for q in (50, 95, 99):
    print(q, round(np.percentile(ms, q)))  # 95, 492, 973
print(round(ms.mean()))            # 157 -- above 65% of your traffic
print(round(np.exp(np.log(ms).mean())))  # 95 -- the geometric mean is the MEDIAN, not the mean

Where this bites in production

Long Term Capital Management, 1998. Models calibrated on normal-tailed volatility gave near-zero probability to a joint Russian default and flight to quality; LTCM lost 4.6 billion dollars in under four months and was recapitalised that September in a 3.6 billion dollar Fed-brokered rescue. The lesson is that tails and correlations are not stable across regimes. The everyday version is Microsoft’s: Bing’s revenue per user has a skewness of 17.9, so a t-test on it needs about 114,000 users per arm before the normal approximation is worth anything.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

You transformed revenue with log1p and the model looks great. How do you report the business impact?
Not by undoing the squash and calling it money. Fitting on the compressed scale gets you the average of the compressed numbers, and un-compressing that gives you something closer to the middle customer than to the average customer — always smaller, sometimes far smaller. Either correct for that with a known adjustment, or fit on the money itself and quote the change in revenue per user with an honest range around it.
Not by exponentiating the coefficient. Fitting on log(1+y) estimates E[log(1+Y)], and exp of that is a geometric mean — systematically below the arithmetic mean that revenue actually is, by roughly a factor of exp(σ2/2) on a lognormal. Either apply Duan’s smearing estimator to retransform, or fit on the raw scale with a heavy-tail-aware model. Then report the lift as a difference in mean revenue per user with a bootstrap interval, because that is the number finance will book.
Your p50 latency is 95 ms, your mean is 157 ms and your p99 is 970 ms. The SLO says "average under 200 ms". What do you do?
Change the promise before you change the system. The target is measuring the wrong thing: the average has plenty of room to spare while one request in a hundred takes ten times the typical wait, and fixing those slow requests barely moves the average at all. Write the promise on the slowest few percent, and pick the threshold from what your system has actually done on past days.
Change the SLO before you change the system. You are passing a target that is blind to the failure: the mean is 157 ms with 43 ms of headroom while one request in a hundred is 970 ms, and no amount of tail improvement or tail degradation will move that headroom much. Rewrite the objective on p95 and p99, set the threshold from a backtest of historical days rather than a round number, and keep the mean as a cost proxy, not a promise.
Bookings per user is heavily right-skewed with a big spike at zero and the team wants a t-test. Your approach?
It depends on one number, and you can go and get it. Measure how lopsided the metric is and work out how many users per arm that lopsidedness demands. Clear that bar and the ordinary test is fine. Miss it and your options are to trim the extreme values at a limit you set in advance, to resample users to get an honest range, or to split the question into who books at all and how much bookers book.
The t-test is not automatically wrong — it is wrong at your sample size. Compute the skewness and compare with 355s2 per arm. If you clear it, Welch is fine and it is a mean, which is what the business wants. If you do not, in order: cap or winsorise at a pre-declared percentile, or bootstrap the difference in means at the user level, or decompose into P(book)×E[bookings∣book] and test both. Do not switch to Mann-Whitney and then report a mean lift.

Say this back tomorrow

Lopsidedness enters the sample size squared. And un-squashing an average never gives you back the average you started with.
n≥355s2  ·  exp(E[logY])=E[Y]
  • The mean of a heavy-tailed metric is set by a handful of rows, so it converges slowly and moves for the wrong reasons
  • Put the SLO on p95 or p99; the mean is a cost proxy, not a promise anyone feels
  • Squared error targets a conditional mean — if you want the middle or the tail, change the loss, not the data

Unlocks

  • skewness and the CLT
  • capping and winsorising
  • quantile regression
  • bootstrap intervals
  • Duan smearing
