Pairing, win rates and the rank that has an interval

Scoring both models on the same prompts turns an inconclusive result into a decision — and a leaderboard position is an interval, not a rank

To find out whether model A beats model B, score them on the same prompts and look at the difference item by item. Most of the noise in an eval is that some prompts are hard, and pairing cancels it: a hard prompt was hard for both. Two separate runs on two different samples throw that away, which is how a real difference ends up looking like nothing.

Worked through. Model A gets 82% and model B gets 79% on the same five hundred prompts. Compare the two scores separately and their ranges overlap, so the honest conclusion is "we could not tell". Compare them prompt by prompt and you find thirty prompts where A was right and B was wrong against fifteen the other way — a difference that comfortably clears the noise. Same data, opposite decision, and the only thing that changed was which comparison you ran.

Like timing two runners. Race them side by side on the same hilly course on the same morning and a two-second gap means something. Time them on different days on different courses and most of the gap is hills and wind. The prompts are the course, and you get to decide whether both runners face the same one.

Two cautions on top. A win rate needs its tie rate printed beside it: winning 55% of the time with four ties in every ten is a different claim from winning 55% with almost no ties. And a leaderboard position is an estimate with a range around it. Put ranges on the scores and three or more models routinely turn out to share a place, so "we are third" usually means "we are somewhere between first and sixth".

Pair whenever the same items can be scored by both systems and test the per-item difference, SE=Var(sA​−sB​)/n​. That removes item difficulty from the variance and is commonly 3–10× more efficient than comparing marginal means. Checking two marginal intervals for overlap is not a test of the difference at all, and it is the most common way a real win gets thrown away.

The arithmetic, because you will be asked to do it out loud. 500 items, A at 82%, B at 79%. Unpaired, the standard error of the difference is 0.82(0.18)/500+0.79(0.21)/500​=2.5pp, so 3 points is 1.2 standard errors and the marginal intervals [78.6,85.4] and [75.4,82.6] overlap. Paired on the very same items — 380 both right, 30 A only, 15 B only — the per-item difference has mean 3pp and SE=1.34pp, giving t=2.25 and p≈0.025.

A win rate is a paired statistic: SE=w(1−w)/n​ on the non-tie subset, with the tie rate reported next to it. Bradley–Terry and Elo compress pairwise outcomes into a scalar but assume conditionally random matchups and a stable model pool, which arena leaderboards routinely violate. For ranks, run directional pairwise tests, apply Holm, and report the set of ranks each model could occupy.

And the leaderboard itself is a selected maximum. The Leaderboard Illusion documented 27 private Llama-4 variants tested pre-release with only the winner disclosed, alongside data-access asymmetry — Google 19.2% and OpenAI 20.4% of all arena data against 29.7% shared between 83 open-weight models — and estimated relative gains of up to 112% on the arena distribution from that access. Best-of-N submission with selective disclosure is the winner’s curse at industry scale.

You reach for it when

  • Two models were scored on the same prompts and their intervals overlap
  • A vendor quotes a 1.2-point lead on a public benchmark
  • Someone reports a 55% win rate and no tie rate
  • Marketing asks what being third on an arena board is worth

The trap

Saying “their ranges overlap, so the two models are the same”. Overlapping ranges are not a test, and when both models answered the same prompts they are the wrong ranges to be looking at. The other one is quoting a leaderboard position as though it were a property of the model rather than a fact about who else happened to be on the board that week.

"The confidence intervals overlap, so the models are the same." Overlapping marginal intervals are not a test of the difference, and when both models were scored on the same items you should never have been looking at the marginal intervals in the first place: on identical numbers the paired test can come back at p = 0.025 while the marginals overlap. The second version is treating an Elo gap as a property of the model when it is a function of which opponents happened to be in the pool that week.

The math requires the same items scored by both systems

SEunpaired​=nσA2​+σB2​​​SEpaired​=nσA2​+σB2​−2ρσA​σB​​​The entire gain is that last term. Two models that fail on the same hard prompts are strongly correlated, and pairing subtracts exactly that correlation. It buys you nothing when the two systems make unrelated errors — which is itself worth knowing.

The same 500 items, two ways scipy

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# 380 both right, 30 only A, 15 only B, 75 neither
A = np.array([1]*380 + [1]*30 + [0]*15 + [0]*75)
B = np.array([1]*380 + [0]*30 + [1]*15 + [0]*75)
print(A.mean(), B.mean())              # 0.82 0.79

print(stats.ttest_ind(A, B, equal_var=False).pvalue)  # 0.232 -- as two separate samples
print(stats.ttest_rel(A, B).pvalue)              # 0.025 -- the same data, paired

# nothing changed but the question: 30 wins against 15 losses,
# and 455 items where both models did the same thing

Where this bites in production

Neuhof & Benjamini, Quantifying Ranking Uncertainty in LLM Benchmarks (arXiv:2607.16259, June 2026), built confidence intervals on ranks over MMLU using PromptEval — 15 models, 57 subjects, 100 prompt variations, paired t-tests with a Holm correction at the 5% level. Two findings worth quoting: subject-level variability substantially exceeds prompt-variant variability, and overlapping intervals routinely put three or more models at the same rank. "We are third" is usually a claim about a group, not a position.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Model A is 1.2 points above Model B on the leaderboard. Is A better?
Not from a leaderboard row. Ask how many items were scored, whether both models saw exactly the same prompts, how much the scores wobble, and whether rewriting the prompt template would move things by more than one and a bit points — it usually would. Recent work that put ranges around leaderboard positions found three or more models sharing a place as a matter of routine. A gap that small is normally inside the wobble.
You cannot tell from a leaderboard row. Four questions: how many items, was the comparison paired on the same prompts, what is the standard error of the difference, and is 1.2 points larger than the swing you would get from a different prompt template? Then the rank question. The June 2026 MMLU rank-uncertainty work — 15 models, 57 subjects, 100 prompt variations — found three or more models routinely sharing a rank once intervals were drawn, and 1.2 points is usually inside that.
Model A 82%, Model B 79% on the same 500 items, and their confidence intervals overlap. Is A better?
Probably yes, and those overlapping ranges are the wrong thing to look at. Both models answered the same five hundred prompts, so the question is not how each scored on its own but how often one beat the other. If A was right on thirty prompts where B was wrong, and B was right on fifteen where A was wrong, that thirty against fifteen is the evidence, and it is strong enough to act on. The separate ranges hid it because most of their width is prompts being hard, which hit both models equally.
Probably yes, and the overlapping intervals are the wrong test. Unpaired, the difference has SE=2.5pp, so 3 points is 1.2 standard errors and the marginals [78.6,85.4] and [75.4,82.6] overlap. But the items are shared: with 380 both right, 30 A only and 15 B only, the per-item difference has mean 3pp and SE=1.34pp, so t=2.25 and p≈0.025. Report the paired test, the win/loss/tie counts, and the interval on the difference.
Your model is third on a public leaderboard. What do you tell the marketing team?
That third place means "in the leading group", and nothing narrower. A rank is a number with a range around it, and when the ranges are drawn, three or more models often share a place. Two further warnings for anyone writing copy: an arena rating depends on which other models happened to be in the pool that week, and teams are allowed to enter many private versions of a model and reveal only the one that did best — one study documented twenty-seven private variants from a single family.
That third means "in the top group", and that is all that goes in writing. Rank is an estimate, so give it an interval: directional pairwise tests with a Holm correction return the set of ranks the model could occupy, and the June 2026 MMLU study found three or more models routinely sharing one. Then two caveats. An Elo number is relative to the opponent pool and moves when the pool changes. And public boards permit best-of-N private submission with only the winner disclosed — 27 private Llama-4 variants in one documented case.

Say this back tomorrow

Score both models on the same prompts and compare them prompt by prompt. Ranges that overlap are not a verdict.
SEpaired​=Var(sA​−sB​)/n​  ·  overlapping marginal intervals are not a test
  • Pair on the same items and test the difference — often 3 to 10 times more efficient
  • Overlapping marginal intervals are not a test of the difference
  • A win rate needs its tie rate printed next to it
  • Ranks have intervals too: three or more models routinely share one
